newsitem.title: UK: Willis "no option" on Sovereign liquidation.
newsitem.headline: Willis "no option" on Sovereign liquidation.

text.p: British broker Willis Corroon Group Plc said on Friday that the impact of an arbitration award between its subsidiary Sovereign Marine and one of its reinsurers could run into tens of millions of pounds.
Earlier the company announced it was putting Sovereign, which has been in run-off since 1991, into liquidation as a result of the arbitration decision.
The move will have no financial impact on Willis itself and potential losses will be borne by Sovereign clients.
But according to Willis director of corporate communications Peter Stevens, the arbitration award could have implications for reinsurance contracts beyond that covered by the arbitration.
At the end of 1996, Sovereign's reinsurance recoveries were valued at 168 million pounds.
The arbitration decision puts this in question.
The eventual impact could be between the 10.2 million pounds of the disputed reinsurance contract which went to arbitration and the 168 million pounds of possible reinsurance recoveries.
"It is going to be sufficiently above the 10.2 million pounds that we didn't have an awful lot of option," said Stevens.

"As a result of the arbitration award, Sovereign had to ask for further unlimited financial support. In those terms it would not have been in shareholders' interests to make those sort of commitments."
Stevens said that Willis hoped the liquidators would in time be able to pay the bulk if not all of Sovereign's liabilities.

The arbitration award meant that adjustment to the disputed treaties had substantially increased Sovereign's liabilities and would have required the provision of additional capital from Willis to avoid liquidation.
Willis decided it could not justify such a commitment.
Losses at Sovereign had cost the group 72 million pounds since it was put into run-off in 1991.
Because of a confidentially clause, Willis was unable to give details of the arbitration which concerned a reinsurer of two of Sovereign's casualty surplus treaties.
But Stevens said the company believed the decision to put Sovereign into liquidation would not effect Willis's ongoing business.

"Professionals in the insurance market understand the business they are in. They understand that Sovereign is only the latest in a long line of companies that has been unable to keep up the pace of the 1980s and will understand that we didn't have any option," said Stevens.
"We don't believe there will be any effect there, our insurance clients will understand the problem and understand we had no alternative.
